newsitem.title: CUBA: Envoy's visit could herald papal talks with Castro.
newsitem.headline: Envoy's visit could herald papal talks with Castro.

text.p: The Vatican's foreign minister Jean-Louis Tauran pays a visit to Cuba on Friday that could pave the way for a meeting between Pope John Paul II and President Fidel Castro and a papal visit to the island.

Tauran is the Vatican's first secretary for relations with states to be invited to Cuba. Both Roman Catholic Church and government sources say his visit comes amid an improvement in relations between the church and the Communist government.

The five-day visit could prepare the ground for a meeting between Castro and the pope when, as is likely, the Cuban leader goes to Rome for a Nov. 13-17 summit organised by the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).

Diplomatic sources in Rome have said recently that if Castro does see the pope he would probably invite him to Cuba, perhaps next year. The island is the only Latin American country the pontiff has not visited.

"It is to be hoped that ... there will be advances in fixing a date for the longed-for visit of His Holiness to our country," Palabra Nueva, a Cuban Catholic Church magazine, said of Tauran's visit in its October edition.
"Tauran's visit is a positive demonstration of willingness and mutual respect in the path of dialogue between the church and the Cuban state," the magazine said.

"The desire of the church is that (Tauran's visit) widens the framework of understanding and respect, as well as enabling a better comprehension of the wide area of work that the church can and should undertake in Cuba," it added.
Officials in the Cuban government and church circles were cautious about predicting a meeting with the pope or a papal visit, noting there was no fixed agenda for Tauran's talks.

Tauran was likely to meet Castro, although this has not been announced. He is scheduled to meet Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina, parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon and local church leaders headed by Cardinal Jaime Ortega.

Church sources noted that Havana will have viewed positively comments made last week by a senior Vatican cardinal, Roger Etchegeray, condemning the recent toughening of the longstanding U.S. embargo against Cuba.
The improvement in church-state relations was illustrated in September when Ortega noted what he called more encouraging comments on religion in a recent Communist Party document.
Cuban authorities moved to more relaxed relations with Christian churches in the early 1990s after years of tension following the 1959 revolution that brought Castro to power.

Membership in the Communist Party is no longer barred to the faithful and 1992 constitutional changes outlawed religious discrimination in clearer terms. But ties with the Catholic Church have been strained at times, particularly over calls by Catholic bishops for political change.

There are still areas of difference, for example on how the church may play a role in society outside the boundaries of church services. While there has been a recent increase in the number of visas granted for foreign priests and nuns to work in Cuba, church sources say they would like to see more.
The Catholic charity Caritas also wants more autonomy, for example to be allowed to run a programme to develop people's skills in small business.
